title: Dutch Angle in AI Video: Prompts and Examples
summary: A Dutch angle tilts the camera so the horizon slants and a scene feels wrong. See real AI video examples, with prompts that hold the tilt, and try it free.
body_markdown:
### What is a Dutch angle in film?


A Dutch angle is a shot where the camera is rolled to one side, so the horizon and other straight lines slant across the frame. Filmmakers use it to make a scene feel tense, unstable or wrong.


### Why is it called a Dutch angle?


The origin of the name is debated. A common explanation is that "Dutch" comes from "Deutsch", the German word for German, since the shot became prominent in German Expressionist films, and it has also been called the German angle.


### What is the difference between a Dutch angle and a canted angle?


There is no difference: Dutch angle, Dutch tilt, canted angle and oblique angle are names for the same shot. A camera tilt is something else, since it points the lens up or down and keeps the horizon level.


### When should you use a Dutch angle?


Use a Dutch angle for a moment when something is off, such as a threat arriving, a character losing control or a quiet argument. It works best when most of the film is level, because too many tilted shots lose their effect.


### How many degrees is a Dutch angle?


There is no fixed number. In our tests, 15 degrees read as a slight lean and 30 degrees as a steep, stormy slant, and 25 degrees was a clear tilt that still left the scene easy to follow.


### How do you prompt a Dutch angle in AI video?


Write the angle, the degrees and the direction in the image prompt, such as "Dutch angle, the whole frame tilted 25 degrees clockwise", then tell the video model to keep the frame tilted for the entire shot and never level out.


### Can a Dutch angle work in animation?


Yes. A Dutch angle works in any style because it depends on lines in the frame, not on a real camera. On this page it appears in a 2D anime test and in Duro, a hand-painted film.
